extracted.intended_audience: marketing and advertising researchers, academic grant reviewers, and methodological researchers interested in consumer behavior and measurement techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for designing, conducting, and interpreting marketing and advertising research (including physiological measurement, multidimensional scaling, computer simulation, and attitude-based choice studies) as reported in grant-funded projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of Research / Social Marketing Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should illustrate applications and evaluate the power of advertising as an instrument of social change; advertising and marketing are treated as neutral instruments that can be applied for social benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize applied demonstrations showing how advertising/marketing can achieve social goals; frame studies to counter value-laden criticisms by showing beneficial applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validity testing for physiological measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical validity testing is a necessary condition for the confident use of physiological measures (e.g., GSR, pupil dilation) in advertising research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do laboratory validity and reliability studies comparing physiological responses to established non-physiological measures before inferring psychological meanings; without such testing, interpretation of physiological responses remains ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of confounding stimulus factors in physiological measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: When using physiological measures such as pupil dilation, control extraneous stimulus properties (e.g., light intensity) so they cannot be alternate explanations for observed physiological changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to eliminate or hold constant alternative stimulus causes; explicitly manipulate and/or control lighting, background, and other contextual variables when attributing physiological responses to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution about physiological responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological responses (e.g., pupil dilation) may index multiple mental states (attention, attraction, fear, etc.), so the meaning of a response is not always clear without empirical validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single-label interpretations of physiological signals; use converging measures and validation studies to specify what a physiological change indicates in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability (lab-to-field external validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory findings must be assessed for their generalizability to the real-world/market context; laboratories provide experimental control but may not reproduce market conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lab studies to effectively simulate the real environment and, where possible, follow up with field tests to verify laboratory insights; explicitly acknowledge risks to external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure selection and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose physiological and non-physiological measures based on literature review and survey of practice; compare physiological measures' responses to multiple non-physiological indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior literature and practitioner surveys to identify commonly used measures and research topics; in experiments, include multiple measurement modalities to triangulate results (e.g., GSR and self-report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity, validity, and reliability of equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the sensitivity, validity, and reliability of physiological measuring equipment (e.g., GSR, PDR) before employing them in substantive research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct calibration, test-retest, and concurrent validity studies; report incidence of use and known limitations from literature and practitioner surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of survey research to inform experimental design
rubrics_metrics.description: Use surveys of practitioners and literature reviews to determine current use patterns and the most frequently studied topics, informing subsequent laboratory experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey marketing research firms, agencies, and corporate research units to prioritize which measures and problems to study experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) methodology and spatial analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply multidimensional scaling to produce metric perceptual/preference spaces from nonmetric data; interpret dimensions as product attributes and distances as dissimilarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pairwise comparisons, rankings, and other nonmetric data; construct perceptual spaces where similarly perceived products occupy similar positions; consider method limitations and explore different scaling algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market segmentation based on perceptual structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Define market segments by individual patterns of perception and preference (perceptual similarity), then segment further by preference position (ideal points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate perceptual segments to socio-economic and demographic variables to make segments actionable for media selection and strategy; explore strategies to 'move' brands in perceptual space or shift consumers' ideal points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relating self-concept to brand preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the relationship between individuals' self-concept and brand preference, acknowledging complexity (actual self vs ideal self) and that simple consistency hypotheses may not always hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure self-concept and map it into perceptual space alongside brands; be open to findings (e.g., preference for aspired/ideal self) and design follow-up studies to clarify mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution interpreting results from small or convenience samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret findings cautiously when sample sizes are small or non-representative (e.g., pilot studies of agency people vs non-experts), as predictive ability may be limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sample sizes and limitations, avoid overgeneralization, and replicate with larger, representative samples before making strong claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation model specification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer simulations require explicit specification of relationships among marketing variables (a model) and estimates of input values; outcomes depend on both model validity and input accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state model assumptions and provide sensitivity analyses to input estimates; recognize that simulation results are conditional on the chosen model structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection criteria and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Model selection should consider trade-offs between model complexity (and associated data requirements/cost) and predictive accuracy; historically choices were convenience-driven but should be formalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance increased accuracy from complex models against higher data costs; adopt formal problem-solving techniques for model selection rather than relying solely on convenience or analyst familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizing model-selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply formal problem-solving and decision techniques to the choice among competing simulation models instead of basing selection on convenience, data availability, or individual skills alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop criteria and procedures for model comparison (e.g., accuracy vs cost), and use them to select the most appropriate model for the marketing decision context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include analyst characteristics in methodological studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that an analyst's background, experience, education, and other characteristics influence model-selection behavior; these can be specified as analyst-types for comparative study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure analyst attributes and, where relevant, include cultural and national characteristics to compare decision behavior across analyst-types and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude-based consumer choice measurement (Fishbein-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model preference/choice as dependent on both the strength of belief that an object possesses attributes and the perceived importance/evaluation of those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect measures of perceived attribute possession, relative importance/evaluation of attributes, and stated preference/choice (including 'ideal' choice); use these to build probabilistic predictive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish structural vs dynamic experimental phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Design studies with a structural phase (measuring relationships among beliefs, attitudes, and choice) and a dynamic phase (examining how advertising and experience change beliefs and choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use laboratory and survey techniques appropriately across phases; structural studies focus on predictive relationships, dynamic studies test media/advertising effects over time or exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic nature of attitude-based predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictions from attitude models are probabilistic: even if a model indicates a first choice, observed behavior may vary (e.g., consumers drink a variety of brands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report predictive probabilities and recognize inherent variability; avoid claiming deterministic prediction of individual choice from attitude measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use attitudinal structure to guide advertising and product strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of belief and attitude structures (including 'ideal' brand attributes) should inform advertising strategy (which attributes to advertise), market segmentation, and product design changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target advertising to change specific beliefs found to influence preference; use attribute- and ideal-based information to select segmentation and design tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare multiple perception/evaluation groups (experts vs non-experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying ad perception/evaluation, compare different evaluator groups (e.g., agency professionals vs non-experts) but be cautious about predictive conclusions when samples are small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comparative studies with adequate sample sizes, and interpret group differences in perceptual structure with caution; include objective performance measures (e.g., coupon returns) where possible.
